displayQuote: I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading!

meta.title: Who really said "I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading!"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Jane Austen wrote it — for a character who is pretending. Caroline Bingley yawns it out to impress Darcy, then throws the book aside.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading!'?
meta.ogDescription: Pride and Prejudice, chapter XI. Spoken by Caroline Bingley, who chose her book only because it was volume two of Darcy’s.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The sentence is Austen’s, in Pride and Prejudice (1813), volume I, chapter XI, and our wording matches the first edition exactly. It is not Austen praising books. The speaker is Caroline Bingley, who has picked up a book only because it is the second volume of the one Darcy is reading, gives up trying to enjoy it, yawns, says this — and two sentences later throws it aside and looks round the room for something else to do.
answer.confidenceText: Verified wording — but read who says it, and why.

source.heading: The passage it comes from

docMeta.dd: London: T. Egerton, 1813, in three volumes
Caroline Bingley — a character, not the narrator

source.excerpt: At length, quite exhausted by the attempt to be amused with her own book, which she had only chosen because it was the second volume of his, she gave a great yawn and said, “How pleasant it is to spend an evening in this way! I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading! How much sooner one tires of any thing than of a book!…” No one made any reply. She then yawned again, threw aside her book, and cast her eyes round the room in quest of some amusement.
trail: Against the first edition — the sentence appears in volume I of the T. Egerton first edition of 1813 ↗, and again in a second scanned copy ↗ of the same edition, both reading “I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading!” with no commas around “after all”.

The punctuation you usually see — the widely circulated Project Gutenberg text ↗ is the illustrated 1894 George Allen edition, which repunctuates the line as “I declare, after all, there is no enjoyment like reading!” Our wording follows 1813.
The chapter — the passage sits in chapter XI, after dinner at Netherfield, in the scene where Miss Bingley is trying and failing to draw Darcy into conversation (Project Gutenberg ↗).
Public domain — first published in 1813, so the text is free of copyright in the United States; Wikisource ↗ and Project Gutenberg both carry it in full.
source.cutTag: Abridged — the omitted clause is about wanting a library of her own
source.excerptNote: Transcribed from the 1813 first edition. The frame is doing all the work: she is bored, the book is a prop, and Austen has her discard it immediately.

author.name: Jane Austen
author.heading: About Jane Austen
author.bio: Jane Austen published four novels in her lifetime, all anonymously — Pride and Prejudice appeared in 1813 as “by the author of Sense and Sensibility”. Her method is almost entirely indirect: characters reveal themselves by what they say and how badly it fits what they are doing. Caroline Bingley declaring her love of reading while yawning over a book she has not chosen is that method in one sentence.

misattribution.heading: The words are real. The sentiment is a performance.
misattribution.intro: This line is everywhere on reading lists, library posters and bookshop tote bags as Jane Austen’s tribute to books. The words are hers. The opinion is not — she gave it to a character precisely so that we would not believe it.

items.why: Austen writes her as bored and calculating: she took the book only because it was the second volume of Darcy’s, and puts it down the moment the remark fails to get his attention.
“No one made any reply. She then yawned again, threw aside her book” — the sentence immediately after is the joke, and quoting the line alone removes it.

items.who: “I declare, after all, there is no enjoyment like reading!”
items.why: The commas come from the 1894 George Allen edition reproduced by Project Gutenberg ↗; the 1813 first edition ↗ has none.

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Austen, genuinely in the novel — and genuinely meant as flattery from a woman who would rather be doing anything else.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Chapter XI is a small masterclass in social manoeuvring. Miss Bingley spends the evening trying to get Darcy to look up from his book, and every device she tries — reading the same title, praising his library, walking about the room — fails in a slightly more visible way than the last.

The declaration about reading is one of those devices. Austen puts an unimpeachable sentiment in the mouth of someone we can see is not sincere, which is a far sharper way of writing about books than simply praising them.
detailsBody: The scene is after dinner at Netherfield, with Jane recovering upstairs. Mr Hurst falls asleep on a sofa; Darcy takes up a book; Miss Bingley takes up the second volume of it and spends more attention on his page than her own.

Two sentences after the famous line she gives up on reading entirely. A few lines further on she is proposing a ball and then walking the length of the room in the hope of being watched — which is when Darcy finally does look up, and not in the way she intended.
context.pull: Austen gave the line to a character so that we would not believe it.

sourcesVerified.claim: The 1813 T. Egerton first edition, volume I, reads "I declare after all there is no enjoyment like reading! How much sooner one tires of any thing than of a book!", spoken after Miss Bingley gives a great yawn, and is followed by "No one made any reply. She then yawned again, threw aside her book".
A second scan of the 1813 first edition carries the same wording, without commas around "after all".

The Project Gutenberg text of Pride and Prejudice (the illustrated 1894 George Allen edition) prints the line in chapter XI as "I declare, after all, there is no enjoyment like reading!", with commas.
Pride and Prejudice was first published in 1813.
Jane Austen lived 1775-1817 and was an English novelist.
